Subject: Private VPC networking follow-up - Acme Corp

Hi Alex / SRE team,

Thanks again for the call today — great to meet you both. Per our discussion, I wanted to capture the high-level outcomes and proposed next steps focused on Private VPC deployment options (PrivateLink vs VPC Peering) and IP allowlists. I've attached a short network diagram and a checklist you can share with your infra team.

Recap / our understanding
- Desired deployment: Private VPC (customer-managed VPC) to isolate inference traffic and keep data on your network.
- Primary question: whether to use AWS VPC Peering or AWS PrivateLink (endpoint service) for connectivity to Redwood's serving plane.
- Controls you need: inbound allowlists, egress proxies/NAT, DNS resolution for endpoint names, and auditability of connections.

Options & trade-offs (short):
- VPC Peering
  - Pros: Simple routing, lower latency, direct private IP connectivity.
  - Cons: Routes need to be managed; cross-account peering setup required; 1:1 peering per region (if you need multi-region).
- AWS PrivateLink (Interface Endpoints)
  - Pros: Per-service private endpoint, security posture good for strict network environments, easier to centralize access via endpoint policies.
  - Cons: Slightly higher egress costs and additional ENIs to manage; DNS configuration required (resolve alias to endpoint).

Networking checklist (high level) - items your SRE team asked about
- Ports/protocols: outbound TLS 443 to Redwood egress ranges (we'll provide exact CIDR list).
- Control plane: The control plane (account & billing) is separate from data path; we use a small set of control endpoints that require outbound HTTPS.
- IP allowlist: We can support both allowlisting Redwood-managed egress IPs and (for PrivateLink) limiting to the interface endpoint.
- NAT/proxies: If you have an outbound proxy, we need to allow it to TLS passthrough or provide proxy credentials for the service account.
- DNS: For PrivateLink we recommend enabling private DNS override so the service hostname resolves to the endpoint IPs.

Next steps
1) Can you confirm which AWS account(s) the VPC(s) will be in and whether you prefer VPC Peering or PrivateLink?
2) If possible, please share a contact for the infra lead (name + email) who will do the networking changes.
3) I'll schedule a technical deep-dive with our infra engineer to walk the SRE team through the diagram and provide the exact IP ranges and template CloudFormation.

Proposed quick timeline
- This week: confirm account IDs + infra contact.
- Next week: technical deep-dive and handoff.

Attachment: acme-redwood-network-diagram.png (simplified)
Attachment: redwood-private-vpc-checklist.pdf

If it helps, I can also include a sample peering request template for your cloud team to submit.

Thanks — looking forward to locking down the approach.

Best,

Thanks Alex — yes, we support PrivateLink for customers who need interface endpoints. A few clarifications and answers for your SRE team: 

1) PrivateLink support (data plane):
- We can publish an AWS Network Load Balancer-backed endpoint service in the region and share the service name with you. Once you create the interface endpoint in your VPC and enable the service, traffic from your VPC to Redwood will stay on the AWS network.
- For customers that prefer peering, we also support VPC Peering in regions where it makes sense. We'll help you determine the best fit in the deep-dive.

2) Control plane connectivity:
- The control plane (auth, billing, management APIs) uses a small set of public HTTPS endpoints. You will need to allow outbound TLS 443 from your management/CI subnets to those endpoints. If you want to restrict control plane traffic, we can provide a short list of FQDNs and IP ranges to allow.

3) Ports / allowlist (example) — please adapt to your firewall change request:
- Data plane (PrivateLink): 443 (TLS) to the interface endpoint (no public IP required).
- Data plane (Peering): 443 (TLS) to private IPs in our serving subnets — we'll provide a CIDR block for the peering session.
- Control plane: 443 (TLS) to: api.redwood.ai, auth.redwood.ai, telemetry.redwood.ai (we will provide exact IP ranges for egress allowlisting).

4) DNS & private DNS:
- For PrivateLink we recommend enabling Private DNS so the service hostname resolves to the endpoint IPs in your VPC. If you prefer to manage DNS yourself, we'll provide the hostname and target IPs for the endpoints.

5) Sample artifacts we'll provide in the deep-dive:
- CloudFormation / Terraform template for creating interface endpoints or peering accept requests.
- Exact CIDR/IP ranges for peering or egress allowlists.
- Example security group rules and route table changes.

6) Next steps (concrete):
- Jordan: can you confirm account ID(s) and a preferred 60-minute slot next week for a technical deep-dive? We'll include one of our infra engineers and Sean for commercial context.
- After the deep-dive we'll deliver the CF/Terraform templates and an annotated checklist for your change request.

I'll schedule the meeting once you confirm availability. Linking the shared checklist and a meeting booking link here: https://meet.redwood.ai/s/priv-vpc-deepdive-acme

If you want, I can also open a POA (permission to act) document so your cloud team can accept the peering/endpoint service quickly.

Best,
Marissa
